source.title: The Fine Line: Navigating Large Language Model Pretraining with Down-streaming Capability Analysis
source.authors: Chen Yang; Jun-Zhuo Li; Xin-Yao Niu; Xin-Run Du; Songyang Gao; Hao-Ran Zhang; Zhao Chen; Xing-Wei Qu; Ruibin Yuan; Yizhi Li; Jia-Heng Liu; Stephen W. Huang; Shawn Yue; Wen-Hu Chen; Jie Fu; Ge Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. The text has an apparent parameter-count inconsistency for DeepSeek-67B: the name and main text indicate 67B, while Appendix A.1 says 670 billion.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits a scaling-law form to downstream benchmark scores across training checkpoints, rather than testing held-out pretraining loss or reproducing the original loss measurements.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law results in Section 5.2 use downstream CEval, CMMLU, and MMLU scores, not held-out cross-entropy loss. The paper also reports other downstream checkpoint trajectories and comparisons in Sections 4 and the appendices; results cited from prior studies are not treated as rows.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 fits a power-law form (Eq. 1) to CEval, CMMLU and MMLU scores across intermediate checkpoints of four LLMs as training tokens grow, and reports how well the fits track the data. This bears on V6 (downstream performance improving predictably with scale/tokens). It does not measure held-out loss, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape or extrapolation. The fits are in-sample, over checkpoints of a single run per model, with no fitted exponents reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors find downstream scores rise with training tokens with diminishing returns, and that Eq.(1) fits some models (Yi-34B, Baichuan2) better than others (DeepSeek). They conclude downstream scaling is nuanced and that downstream metrics diverge from loss-based laws. The paper's main framing is checkpoint-level capability dynamics (cross-task prediction, curriculum-like cross-domain ordering) more than scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits a scaling-law form to downstream benchmark scores over existing model checkpoints rather than measuring held-out loss in controlled size, data, and compute sweeps. It describes the scaling-law approaches used by the models as differing: Baichuan2 uses a Henighan et al. approach, while DeepSeek uses an IsoFLOP-profile approach with modifications.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit quality differs by model; the text also notes possible differences between early and late training and discusses use of non-embedding FLOPs per token versus overall parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: Trajectories of MMLU, CMMLU and CEval co-move within each model across checkpoints. Authors say known-task dynamics predict unseen tasks in the same domain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-domain downstream benchmarks share training dynamics, so one can forecast another during pretraining.

record.problems: Section 5.2 presents fit curves as figures without numerical fit coefficients or uncertainty estimates. The paper acknowledges imperfect fit and uses downstream scores rather than held-out loss. The text also gives an inconsistent DeepSeek-67B parameter count in Appendix A.1.
record.rows_left_out: The additional checkpoint-by-benchmark trajectories in Figures 1–5 and 7–11 and Tables 2–9 are not itemized here; Section 5.2 Figure 6 is the paper's direct scaling-law fit analysis, while the other results are broader downstream capability trajectories.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs. The Eq.(1) fits are in-sample only.
Compute-optimal allocation is only discussed via prior work, not estimated.
There is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
No other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning are studied.

Untested: downstream performance versus pretraining loss; out-of-sample prediction; fitting across model sizes rather than across tokens within one run; tasks other than the three exam benchmarks in the fit.

No fitted exponents are reported, and no parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting-method choices are varied. Differences in fit quality across models are attributed speculatively (e.g. non-embedding FLOPs), not tested.

missing.what: Numeric checkpoint scores for every Figure 6 series. The rows wrongly say 'figure only'.
Cross-scale comparison: at equal tokens, 67B > 34B > 7B on math tasks, but OpenLLaMA-7B approaches or exceeds Yi-34B (qualitative, from figures).

Non-smooth trajectories. Amber-7B and OpenLLaMA-7B MMLU sit near chance (about 25) for hundreds of billions of tokens before rising. Amber-7B code ability declines at 200-300B tokens. Commonsense benchmarks plateau early (before about 300B).

record.verdict_notes: The fits are within single training runs (checkpoints under one LR schedule), not across independently trained models. No coefficients or goodness-of-fit numbers are given, so 'fits closely' rests on visual judgement. The text's claim of monotonic increase is contradicted by the tables (e.g. Yi-34B CMMLU). Appendix A.1 misstates the DeepSeek sizes as 70B/670B. V7 links were removed because the rows measure downstream fit quality, not exponent or split dependence on setup choices.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not report fitting on small runs and evaluating predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It discusses disagreements in compute-optimal allocation but does not test an allocation or estimate parameter/token growth with compute.
It does not isolate architecture details at fixed parameter count and compare their effect on loss.
The evaluated results are language-model downstream benchmarks; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
It evaluates downstream benchmark scores across training-token checkpoints, but does not test downstream performance against held-out pretraining loss or cover all downstream tasks.

It reports differences in fit quality across models and notes departures from the expected trajectory, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, fitting method, or compute-optimal allocation.

relationships.condition: Baichuan2-7B (CEval, CMMLU, MMLU) and Yi-34B (CEval, MMLU), score versus training tokens within each run
relationships.reason: Scores rise with diminishing returns, and the authors say Eq.(1) fits these models most closely (Tables 2, 7-8; r1, r2, r3, r10, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increase with diminishing returns as training tokens accumulate, and the authors identify their proposed equation as the closest fit for these model runs.

relationships.condition: DeepSeek-7B and DeepSeek-67B on all three benchmarks; Yi-34B on CMMLU
relationships.reason: The authors say the DeepSeek fits deviate from Eq.(1). DeepSeek-7B stays near chance until about 800-1000B tokens, then jumps. Yi-34B CMMLU swings by up to 20 points between checkpoints (r4-r9, r11).
relationships.display_finding: DeepSeek fits deviated from the proposed law, with DeepSeek-7B near chance until about 800–1000B tokens before jumping, while Yi-34B CMMLU fluctuated by up to 20 points.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
